about.heading: About
paragraphs: Krina Patel has lived this conviction throughout her career. It began in Ahmedabad with UTSAH, a creative arts program designed with the disability community and open to every student. It continued in classrooms in New York City and Boston, where her students explored identity through portraits and stories. In her work in the community and the schools, she saw that engaging the body and the senses enhances learning, and is perhaps essential for some students. Her doctoral research at Harvard, on how artisans think and learn, gave the conviction its evidence: thinking is an embodied process engaging the body, brain and mind.

In time, the work moved into community life. STIR A MEMORY began with food as a way into memories and stories, and grew into Memories are Stories™, projects that invite people to share their stories and connect with one another. Because connection matters to health, she has collaborated with healthcare providers and community health organizations to design arts programs that address social isolation.

Throughout, her studio practice has continued, from drawing and printmaking at the Kanoria Centre for Arts in Ahmedabad and the Art Students League in New York to the prints and collage she makes today in traditional and digital media.

Her book An Artwork a Day: The Arts in Health and Wellbeing brings these strands together in one argument: small daily acts of sensory attention and creative expression are essential to health and wellbeing. That argument now extends into policy and evaluation in the arts sector, and into talks and workshops on everyday creativity, on finding awe and wonder in everyday places.
italics: An Artwork a Day: The Arts in Health and Wellbeing

studio.heading: Studio
paragraphs: My practice begins with the line. I try to convey the look and feel of what I am remembering, reflecting on and observing: a visual gestalt, an essence. I expand on that through further work, working both digitally and with physical materials, layering until the work holds more than the line alone.

These layers and fragments of images are rarely neutral. They are drawn from various sources and made by hand. They come together to express the sense of a time, a place, the people who were there. Layering images is a way of layering memory: each piece I add is a story that connects me back to a self, a place, people.

Through my work, I am pursuing a question of connection: to self, to the outside world, to people, to place, to objects. I make this work to trace that connection for myself, and to invite viewers to trace their own.

research.heading: Research
research.title: From the Sky to the Loom
paragraphs: I believe the urge to make is innate. It lives in the vegetable vendor’s pushcart and the henna-patterned palm as much as in the gallery, and it grows with practice. Growing up in India, I was surrounded by this everyday art, made by ordinary people going about their lives.

Art and craft were once one idea. H. Kumar Vyas, one of the founders of the National Institute of Design, writes, “no separate terms were needed to distinguish the [plastic] arts from the crafts. In the minds of the creators and the people for whom these objects were created, art and craft remain one inseparable concept.” Fine art as a realm of its own, Larry Shiner shows, took shape in Europe in the early nineteenth century, and reached India with the art gallery in the 1930s.

A line of Indian artists and educators held on to the idea of crafts and arts as one unified concept and built institutions around it: Tagore and Nandalal Bose at Santiniketan, K.G. Subramanyan, Dashrath Patel, and the founders of NID. They understood creativity as a capacity everyone carries, and art, craft and design as one practice.

From the Sky to the Loom is my research into what that inheritance means today. Kabir, in Tagore’s translation, speaks of the inward and the outward becoming one sky*. I am asking what that one sky looks like now, when a contemporary artist carries craft into the Venice Biennale as a choice, and an artisan works the loom to live.

I am bringing these two strands together in two ways. I am interviewing contemporary artists about how they hold freedom and labor in their own practice. And I am reading the writings of Tagore, Bose, Subramanyan, Patel and Vyas, to set what artists tell me today alongside what these thinkers set out to build. The research, once again, hews to the idea of the whole that underlies my work.
italics: From the Sky to the Loom
research.note: * The line comes from poem XVII of Songs of Kabir, translated by Tagore and published by Macmillan in New York in 1915. The full passage reads:
research.note_quote: I have known in my body the sport of the universe: I have escaped from the error of this world. The inward and the outward are become as one sky, the Infinite and the finite are united: I am drunken with the sight of this All!
